collections.title: Number Theory · Arithmetic, Congruences, and First Prime Questions
collections.summary: Start with integer arithmetic and modular reasoning, then meet three questions about solutions, squares, and primes. Continue into one of the focused branches rather than treating all advanced arithmetic as one required sequence.

chapters.title: Divisibility, reconstruction, and multiplicative order
Integer solutions, quadratic residues, and prime distribution

assumed_background: Integer arithmetic, fractions, equations, and school algebra. Proof habits help; no prior group theory or analytic number theory is assumed.

collections.title: Number Theory · Rational Approximation and Pell Equations

chapters.title: Integer parametrization and approximation
Periodic continued fractions and the complete Pell theorem

assumed_background: Euclidean algorithm, fractions, elementary algebra, and inequalities. The first survey lecture supplies gcd and divisibility.

collections.title: Number Theory · Reciprocity, Sums of Squares, and Counting

chapters.title: Quadratic residues and a proof of reciprocity
From multiplicative functions to two-square counts
A geometric comparison: lattice points in a circle

assumed_background: Congruences, multiplicative order, and elementary proof methods. Gaussian integers and arithmetic functions are developed in the selected lectures; the lattice-point comparison uses areas and elementary estimates.

collections.title: Number Theory · Finite Fields and Primality Certificates

chapters.title: Orders, witnesses, and finite-field examples
Construction, uniqueness, Frobenius, and irreducibility

assumed_background: Divisibility, congruences, modular inverses, and elementary polynomial algebra. The survey supplies the integer arithmetic; the selected lectures develop field construction.

collections.title: Number Theory · Dirichlet and the Prime Number Theorem

chapters.title: Counting functions, characters, and Euler products
Complex tools, continuation, and nonvanishing
Primes in progressions and the size of prime counts
The zero-free line, a Tauberian argument, and the prime number theorem

assumed_background: Congruences, elementary proof methods, single-variable calculus, convergent series, and basic complex numbers. Lecture 015000 develops series and partial summation; 026000 supplies contours and Cauchy theory before their later use. The full complex-analysis course offers more patient background.

collections.title: Number Theory · Integers, Ideals, and Class Groups
collections.summary: Ideal-factorization and norm foundations precede the class-group calculation that uses them. This is a proof-led route; the original source order remains available.

chapters.title: Factorization works, then fails
Dedekind foundations, ideal factorization, and multiplicative norms
A class-group calculation and prime splitting

assumed_background: Rings, ideals, modules, finite field extensions, and elementary linear algebra. The selected lectures build the number-field arguments. Minkowski’s lattice calculation uses geometric volume estimates; finite fields help with residue degrees.

collections.title: Number Theory · Quadratic Forms and Prime Representation

chapters.title: From ideal lattices to reduced forms and class numbers
Which primes can the form represent?

assumed_background: Quadratic fields, ideal classes, multiplicative ideal norms, prime splitting, and quadratic reciprocity. These are supplied by the algebraic-integers and reciprocity branches.

collections.title: Number Theory · p-Adic Fields, Norms, and Hilbert Symbols
collections.summary: Begin with lifting, distance, completion, and exact roots. Later stages build general extensions and Hilbert symbols using ideal theory and reciprocity; the chapters make those background changes visible.

chapters.title: Finite lifting, p-adic distance, completion, and compatible residues
Exact roots, local squares, and quadratic extensions
General extensions, residue fields, and ramification
Hilbert symbols, local forms, and rational reciprocity

assumed_background: Congruences and finite fields; Cauchy sequences and completeness; polynomial field extensions. The general-extension stage also uses Dedekind ideal structure. Quadratic reciprocity is used for the final rational Hilbert-reciprocity theorem. Hasse–Minkowski is not proved by this route.
